title: Comparative Evaluation of NaCl and K2SO4‐Assisted Electrochemical Oxidation Coupled With Biodegradation for Textile Effluent Treatment
content:
A combined electrochemical oxidation–biodegradation strategy efficiently treated azo dye-containing textile effluent. NaCl-assisted oxidation using a Ti/TiO2–RuO2–IrO2 anode, followed by biodegradation with Enterobacter hormaechei and Stutzerimonas stutzeri, enhanced dye degradation, decolorization, COD reduction, and detoxification, demonstrating an effective integrated approach for textile wastewater remediation.


ABSTRACT

Azo dye discharge from textile effluent is a life-threatening hazard that affects the environment due to its high accumulation. The present study focuses on a dual treatment approach combining both aerobic and electrochemical treatment for an efficient remediation of textile discharges. NaCl and K2SO4 have been used as electrolytes with TiO2–RuO2–IrO2 anode under galvanic conditions at different concentrations varying from 0.1 to 0.5 g. Initial degradation and decolorization have been confirmed using UV–Vis spectroscopy and FTIR analysis, revealing the breakdown of azo dyes from textile wastewater. Structural degradation of azo dyes was investigated using GC–MS spectrum analysis, which reveals the production of intermediates through fragmentation and mineralization confirming degradation. NaCl-mediated electrochemical oxidation (EO) provided better degradation by producing active chlorine, whereas K2SO4-mediated produced free radical-mediated oxidation with slightly lesser degradation comparatively. EO treatment enhanced thedegradation of effluent and exposure of Enterobacter hormaechei and Stutzerimonas stutzeri enables effective biodegradation of the effluent. EO yielded almost full decolorization (> 99%) and significant COD reduction (~90%). Following this, after 7 days of aerobic biodegradation, the optical density of the NaCl-pretreated wastewater at 600 nm wavelength (OD600) rose from 0.06 to 1.50, which indicated improved microbial activity due to the electrochemical treatment. This study has proven that combining EO with bacterial biodegradation can improve color removal and reduce the organic load of textile effluent, with treatment performance influenced by the supporting electrolyte.
